name: Emu oil

card.summary: An oil rendered from emu fat, rich in oleic and linoleic acids, used as a topical moisturiser and for skin, scars and hair care to leave skin softer and better conditioned.
card.note: Supplements and 'pure emu oil' products are unstandardised; the FDA noted in 2009 that many are unapproved drug claims.

quick.overview:
Emu oil is rendered from the body fat of the emu, a flightless Australian bird. It is mostly unsaturated fat, with oleic acid the largest component, followed by linoleic acid. People apply it to skin as a moisturiser and use it on scars, dry patches and sometimes hair, hoping for softer, better-conditioned skin.
It has a long reported history in Aboriginal Australian medicine and is sold in cosmetics and supplement capsules. Human studies are few and small: a 1996 pilot examined its moisturising and cosmetic properties, trials in cancer patients tested it for radiation dermatitis and joint pain, and a systematic review found it equivalent or less effective than standard care for radiodermatitis.
quick.how: It is used as a topical oil or as an ingredient in creams, and also sold as capsules. Product colour and thickness vary from creamy off-white to a thin yellow liquid depending on diet and refining. A looksmax.org member asked whether emu oil capsules are a useful vitamin K2 source.
quick.risks: No serious harms are highlighted, but products are not standardised and potency varies. The FDA noted in 2009 that many 'pure emu oil' products make drug claims without approval. As with any topical oil, skin reactions are possible.

lead: Emu oil is rendered from the body fat of the emu (Dromaius novaehollandiae), a flightless bird native to Australia. Colour and thickness vary from creamy off-white to a thin yellow liquid depending on the bird's diet and refining. Refined oil is at least 70 percent unsaturated fatty acids, mostly oleic acid, with roughly 20 percent linoleic acid and 1-2 percent linolenic acid [1][2].

People use it as a topical emollient: rubbed into dry skin, around scars and healing areas, and sometimes into hair and scalp, with the aim of leaving skin softer, better conditioned and more supple. It is also an ingredient in creams and is sold in capsules. Proponents point to its use in Aboriginal Australian medicine and to its penetration-enhancing and anti-inflammatory properties [1][2][3].

Human research consists of small trials on moisturisation, radiation skin reactions, nipple skin and joint pain, alongside animal studies of inflammation [3][4][5][6][7]. The FDA has noted that many products sold as pure emu oil are unapproved drugs when marketed with treatment claims [1].

chain: Occlusive and emollient conditioning of the surface
Skin feels softer and looks better moisturised
angle.text: People apply emu oil as an emollient on dry skin, scars and sometimes hair, expecting softer, more conditioned skin. Evidence for appearance outcomes rests on small pilot work.

paras: The oil comes from fat deposits on the bird's back and body, rendered by heating and filtering. Refining removes proteins and water and yields a pale, neutral-smelling oil [1][2]. Industrial oil is at least 70 percent unsaturated fatty acids [1]. Grokipedia describes two rendering approaches, wet rendering in hot water and dry rendering, and notes that oil is mainly a by-product of emu farming for meat [2].
The American Emu Association publishes a trade rule defining grades and quality standards for emu oil used for different purposes, since commercial products are not otherwise standardised [1].

Oleic acid (omega-9) is the largest component, followed by linoleic acid (omega-6) and a small share of linolenic acid (omega-3) [1]. Reviews describe the oil as containing polyunsaturated fat and antioxidants, and suggest its fatty acids could act on cyclooxygenase, lipoxygenase and lipoxin pathways, although the review states that its mechanisms have not been studied directly [3].

Cosmetic use is as a topical moisturiser and in creams. Reviews describe cosmetic activity, transdermal penetration-enhancing activity and traditional topical use for inflammation [3]. Practitioners apply it to dry skin, scars and sometimes hair, expecting a softer, more conditioned look and feel.

It has also been promoted as an oral supplement for conditions such as arthritis; Wikipedia describes the supplement claims as unsupported [1]. Reviews of emu products discuss topical and oral use for mucositis, bowel inflammation and auricular inflammation [3][12].
A 1996 double-blind pilot study in the Australasian Journal of Dermatology examined moisturising and cosmetic properties of emu oil [4].

A randomised placebo-controlled pilot study of processed emu oil examined prevention of radiation dermatitis [5]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of radiodermatitis interventions, which informed Oncology Nursing Society guidelines, concluded that aloe vera and emu oil were equivalent or less effective than standard care [6][13]. A phase II placebo-controlled trial of topical emu oil for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain in 73 women found no statistically significant benefit over placebo oil, although pain improved in both groups over eight weeks [7]. A Cochrane review of systemic therapies for aromatase-inhibitor musculoskeletal symptoms covers the same condition by other routes [14]. A trial in breastfeeding women assessed emu oil on areola skin [8].

Animal studies of emu oil in colitis and atopic-dermatitis-like skin responses have been published [9][10], and a narrative review lists emu oil among lipid-based products examined for chemotherapy-induced intestinal mucositis [12].

Community material is sparse. A looksmax.org thread asks whether emu oil capsules, said to be a vitamin K2 (MK-4) source, are preferable to ordinary K2 capsules; replies suggested standard K2 capsules or hard cheeses as alternatives [11].
Supplements are not standardised and vary in potency. In 2009 the FDA noted that many pure emu oil products are unapproved drugs [1]. As with other topical oils, skin reactions are possible.

lore.intro: Discussion in looksmaxxing forums is thin; one looksmax.org thread concerns emu oil capsules as a vitamin K2 source [11].

claims.claim: Emu oil capsules are a good vitamin K2 (MK-4) source
claims.believers: A poster says the capsules are said to be high in K2 and asks whether they beat standard K2 [11].
claims.experts: Emu oil's fatty acid profile is described, and its vitamin K2 content is not reported.

claims.claim: Emu oil is a skin moisturiser and anti-inflammatory
claims.believers: Marketing and traditional use attribute moisturising and healing properties to it [1][3].
claims.experts: A review reports anti-inflammatory actions; a radiodermatitis meta-analysis found it equivalent or less effective than standard care [3][6].

claims.claim: Emu oil helps scars and wound healing
claims.believers: Traditional Aboriginal use and marketing attribute healing properties to it [1][2].
claims.experts: Published work is mostly animal or small trials; the radiodermatitis meta-analysis found it equivalent or less effective than standard care [6].

claims.claim: Emu oil eases joint pain when rubbed on
claims.believers: Marketing and traditional use describe it as an anti-inflammatory rub [3].
claims.experts: In the JUST trial, emu oil showed no significant benefit over placebo oil, though both groups improved [7].
